statement: David Lewis-Williams (with Thomas Dowson) proposed the "neuropsychological model" — that San rock art motifs (geometric "entoptic" forms and therianthropes) represent imagery experienced during trance/altered states, based on analogy to 19th-20th century San ethnography, including both the Bleek-Lloyd /Xam material and later Kalahari (Ju/'hoansi) trance-dance ethnography. Anne Solomon directly disputes this, arguing Lewis-Williams elides /Xam (Cape, 19th century) and Kalahari San (20th century) ethnography into a single narrative, and that there is no clear evidence the historical /Xam themselves connected dance/trance states with healing in the way the Kalahari material documents. Mathias Guenther (Tricksters and Trancers, Indiana UP, 1999) takes a qualified middle position, accepting "shaman" as broadly appropriate terminology while emphasizing ambiguity and cultural variability over a single fixed reading.
scholarly_disagreement: Whether San rock art imagery can be confidently linked to specific documented trance/healing cosmological content, and whether /Xam and Kalahari San ethnographic material can be combined for this purpose.

sources.citation: Lewis-Williams, David, and Thomas Dowson. "The Signs of All Times: Entoptic Phenomena in Upper Palaeolithic Art." Current Anthropology 29:2, 1988.
sources.author: Lewis-Williams and Dowson

sources.citation: Solomon, Anne. "The southern San and the trance dance: a pivotal debate in the interpretation of San rock paintings." Antiquity.
sources.author: Anne Solomon

interpretations.position: San rock art imagery represents trance/altered-state experience, per a neuropsychological model applicable across San groups and periods
interpretations.strongest_case: 19th-20th century San ethnography (Bleek-Lloyd plus Kalahari) supports the trance-dance interpretive framework, per Lewis-Williams and Pearce's continued defense.

interpretations.position: The trance-dance link elides genuinely distinct /Xam and Kalahari San evidentiary bases and overstates continuity
interpretations.strongest_case: No clear evidence the historical /Xam themselves connected dance/trance states with healing in the way later Kalahari material documents — Lewis-Williams's model conflates two different groups and centuries.
